title: A Letter to God + Dust of Snow + Fire and Ice — Chapter Summary
intro: Chapter 1 of First Flight pairs a short story with two short poems. The prose is 'A Letter to God' by Gregorio López y Fuentes — a Mexican farmer Lencho writes to God for 100 pesos after a hailstorm and the post-office staff, moved by his faith, send 70 pesos as a reply. The poems are by Robert Frost: 'Dust of Snow' captures a tiny moment that lifts a sad mood, and 'Fire and Ice' argues that human emotions — desire and hate — are the forces capable of ending a world.

sections.heading: A Letter to God — Plot
bullets: Lencho is a farmer on a small hill in Mexico; his cornfield needs rain.
Heavy rain comes — but turns into hailstones the size of acorns; the field is destroyed.
Lencho's only hope is God; he writes to Him asking for 100 pesos to plant his fields again.
The postmaster, moved by Lencho's faith, asks his employees to contribute and adds his own salary; they collect 70 pesos.
The reply envelope is signed simply 'God'.
Lencho counts the money, finds 30 pesos missing, and accuses the post-office staff of being 'a bunch of crooks'.

sections.heading: A Letter to God — Themes
bullets: UNSHAKEABLE FAITH — Lencho writes directly to God.
HUMAN COMPASSION — the postmaster and staff respond practically.
IRONY — the readers see what Lencho cannot.
PERCEPTION VS REALITY — Lencho is so trapped in his world-view that he misreads kindness as theft.
NATURE — friend (rain) and foe (hail) in one storm.

sections.heading: Dust of Snow — Meaning
bullets: Frost's eight-line poem about a tiny moment: a crow shakes snow off a hemlock tree onto the speaker.
The cold flakes lift the speaker's mood — a part of a 'rued' day is saved.
Theme: SMALL THINGS — even from gloomy sources — can heal.
Symbols: crow + hemlock are usually 'dark', but here deliver JOY (a quiet reversal).
Form: two stanzas of four lines each, ABAB CDCD rhyme scheme.

sections.heading: Fire and Ice — Argument
bullets: Frost asks how the world will end — fire or ice?
Speaker first sides with fire (desire); but knows enough of hate to say ice would suffice too.
FIRE = DESIRE (hot, consuming, all-or-nothing).
ICE = HATE (cold, slow, deadening).
Both, as HUMAN emotions, are equally capable of destroying a world.
Form: nine short lines, conversational tone, irregular rhyme.

sections.heading: What Unifies the Chapter
bullets: All three pieces explore HUMAN NATURE through small encounters.
Story: small EVENTS (a hailstorm, a letter, a misjudgement) change everything.
Dust of Snow: small NATURAL MOMENTS heal mood.
Fire and Ice: small INNER EMOTIONS, fed and unchecked, can destroy worlds.
Common message: small things have great power in human life.

key_takeaways: 'A Letter to God' (López y Fuentes) — faith, compassion and the ironic gap between perception and reality.
Lencho's faith moves the postmaster to organise a collection of 70 pesos, signed 'God'.
The story's climax: Lencho, ungrateful, accuses the helpers of theft.
'Dust of Snow' (Frost) — a crow shaking snow off a hemlock unexpectedly lifts the speaker's mood.
Dark symbols (crow, hemlock) deliver joy — a quiet reversal.
'Fire and Ice' (Frost) — both desire and hate are equally destructive.
Human emotions, not natural disasters, are the forces that end a world.
Across the chapter: small things — events, moments, emotions — have great power in human life.
